questions.stem: A Bernoulli random variable models:
options: a fixed number of trials, counting the total number of successes
the number of trials needed until the first success occurs
a single trial with any number of equally likely outcomes
a single trial with two outcomes, success (X = 1) and failure (X = 0)
questions.explanation: A Bernoulli trial has just two outcomes, coded X = 1 for success with probability p and X = 0 for failure with probability q = 1 − p. Counting successes over n such trials gives a binomial variable instead.

questions.stem: A Bernoulli random variable has P(X = 1) = 0.3. Its mean and variance are:
questions.explanation: For a Bernoulli variable, E(X) = p = 0.3 and Var(X) = p(1 − p) = 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.21. Squaring p gives 0.09, which is E(X)², not the variance.

questions.stem: A basketballer scores each free throw with probability 0.8. X = 1 if she scores her next free throw and X = 0 if not. The standard deviation of X is:
questions.explanation: X is Bernoulli with p = 0.8, so Var(X) = 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.16 and the standard deviation is √0.16 = 0.4. The value 0.16 is the variance, not the standard deviation.

questions.stem: The variance p(1 − p) of a Bernoulli random variable is greatest when p equals:
questions.explanation: p(1 − p) = p − p² is a parabola with zeros at p = 0 and p = 1, so its maximum is halfway, at p = 1/2, where the variance is 1/4. At p = 0 or 1 the outcome is certain and the variance is 0.

questions.stem: A Bernoulli random variable has variance 0.24, and its probability of success p is less than 0.5. The value of p is:
questions.explanation: p(1 − p) = 0.24 gives p² − p + 0.24 = 0, so (p − 0.4)(p − 0.6) = 0. Since p < 0.5, p = 0.4. The value 0.6 also gives variance 0.24 but breaks the condition.

questions.stem: Which situation can be modelled by a binomial distribution?
options: Drawing 5 cards from a deck without replacement and counting the hearts
Rolling a die until a six appears and counting the rolls needed
Rolling 5 dice and adding up the numbers shown on them
Drawing 5 cards from a deck with replacement and counting the hearts
questions.explanation: A binomial variable counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with the same probability of success. With replacement, each draw has P(heart) = 1/4. Without replacement the probability changes from draw to draw, so the trials are not independent.

questions.stem: Three balls are drawn without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 5 blue balls, and X is the number of red balls. Why is X not binomial?
options: The probability of red is exactly 1/2, so the outcome is certain
The probability of red changes from draw to draw, so the trials are not independent
There are more than two possible colours that could be drawn from the bag
The number of draws is not fixed in advance, so n is unknown
questions.explanation: After a red ball is removed, P(red) on the next draw is 4/9, not 5/10, so the trials are dependent and p is not constant. There are only two colours and n = 3 is fixed, so those conditions are met.

questions.stem: In X ~ Bin(n, p), the factor C(n, r) in P(X = r) counts:
options: the number of trials needed to obtain r successes
the number of failures that occur among the n trials
the number of orders in which r successes can occur in n trials
the probability that the first r trials are all successes
questions.explanation: Each particular sequence of r successes and n − r failures has probability p^r(1 − p)^(n − r). There are C(n, r) ways to choose which r trials are the successes, so the probabilities are multiplied by C(n, r).

questions.stem: If X ~ Bin(10, 0.35), then P(X = 4) is:
questions.explanation: P(X = r) = C(n, r)p^r(1 − p)^(n − r) with n = 10, r = 4 and p = 0.35. Leaving out C(10, 4) gives the probability of just one particular order, and the failures (0.65)⁶ must be included.

questions.stem: If X ~ Bin(12, 0.25), then E(X) equals:
questions.explanation: E(X) = np = 12 × 0.25 = 3. The value 2.25 is the variance, np(1 − p) = 3 × 0.75.

questions.stem: If X ~ Bin(20, 0.4), then Var(X) equals:
questions.explanation: Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 20 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 4.8. The value 8 is the mean np, and about 2.19 is the standard deviation √4.8.

questions.stem: If X ~ Bin(10, 0.1), then P(X = 0) is:
questions.explanation: X = 0 means every one of the 10 trials is a failure, each with probability 0.9, so P(X = 0) = 0.9¹⁰. The expression 10 × 0.1 × 0.9⁹ is P(X = 1), and 1 − 0.9¹⁰ is P(X ≥ 1).

questions.stem: If X ~ Bin(4, 1/3), then P(X = 2) is:
If X ~ Bin(5, 0.2), then P(X ≥ 1) is:
questions.explanation: P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − 0.8⁵. The value 0.8⁵ is P(X = 0) itself, and 5 × 0.2 × 0.8⁴ is only P(X = 1).

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed 6 times. The probability of at most one head is:
questions.explanation: X ~ Bin(6, 1/2), so P(X ≤ 1) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) = (1 + 6)/64 = 7/64. Counting only exactly one head gives 6/64 = 3/32.

questions.stem: Three fair coins are tossed and the number of heads is recorded. This is repeated 80 times. The expected number of times exactly 2 heads are obtained is:
questions.explanation: For X ~ Bin(3, 1/2), P(X = 2) = 3/8. The expected frequency is 80 × 3/8 = 30. Taking P(X = 2) as 1/2 gives 40.

questions.stem: A student guesses every answer in a 20-question test with 4 options per question. The mean and variance of the number correct are:
questions.explanation: X ~ Bin(20, 1/4), so E(X) = 20 × 1/4 = 5 and Var(X) = 20 × 1/4 × 3/4 = 3.75. Using 1 − p in place of p(1 − p) gives 15.

questions.stem: 4% of the items from a machine are faulty. For a random sample of 25 items, the standard deviation of the number of faulty items is:
questions.explanation: X ~ Bin(25, 0.04), so Var(X) = 25 × 0.04 × 0.96 = 0.96 and the standard deviation is √0.96, a little under 1. The mean is 1, which is np, not the standard deviation.

questions.stem: A binomial random variable X has mean 6 and variance 4.2. Its parameters are:
questions.explanation: np = 6 and np(1 − p) = 4.2, so dividing gives 1 − p = 0.7 and p = 0.3, then n = 6/0.3 = 20. Taking p = 0.7 confuses p with 1 − p and gives a mean of 14.

questions.stem: Each trial has success probability 0.2. What is the smallest number of independent trials for the probability of at least one success to exceed 0.9?
questions.explanation: We need 1 − 0.8ⁿ > 0.9, so 0.8ⁿ < 0.1. 0.8¹⁰ ≈ 0.107, which is still too big, and 0.8¹¹ ≈ 0.086, so n = 11. Five trials only make the expected number of successes 1.

questions.stem: X ~ Bin(7, p) with 0 < p < 1, and P(X = 3) = P(X = 4). The value of p is:
questions.explanation: C(7, 3)p³(1 − p)⁴ = C(7, 4)p⁴(1 − p)³, and C(7, 3) = C(7, 4) = 35, so 1 − p = p and p = 1/2. The distribution of Bin(7, 1/2) is symmetric about 3.5.

questions.stem: In statistics, a population is:
options: the number of people who respond to a survey question
the group of people who live in a particular region
the entire group of people or objects about which information is sought
a selection of people or objects drawn from a larger group
questions.explanation: The population is the whole group being studied. A sample is a selection drawn from it, used because measuring the whole population is often impractical.

questions.stem: A statistic from a sample is usually a good approximation to the population value when the sample is random and:
options: it is taken from a single location
its size is exactly 10% of the population
its size is large enough, typically n ≥ 30
questions.explanation: Random selection avoids bias, and a large enough sample, typically n ≥ 30, reduces the effect of chance variation. Choosing only typical members would bias the sample.

questions.stem: For a sample X₁, X₂, ..., Xₙ, the sample mean X̄ is:
options: the middle value of X₁, X₂, ..., Xₙ
questions.explanation: X̄ = (1/n) × ΣXᵢ, the sum of the sample values divided by the sample size. The middle value is the median, a different statistic.

questions.stem: Two random samples of the same size are taken from a population and have different sample means. This shows that:
options: the samples were too large to give the same mean as each other
sample means vary from sample to sample, so X̄ is a random variable
at least one of the two samples must have been chosen incorrectly
the population mean must have changed between the two samples
questions.explanation: Different random samples contain different individuals, so their means usually differ. That variation is why X̄ has a distribution of its own, the sampling distribution of the mean.

questions.stem: For a given sample size n, the sampling distribution of the mean is:
options: the distribution of the whole population being sampled
the list of sample sizes needed to estimate the mean
the distribution of the means of all possible samples of size n
the distribution of the values within one sample of size n
questions.explanation: Take every possible sample of size n, find each one's mean, and look at how those means are distributed. That is different from the spread of values within a single sample.

questions.stem: A random sample of 200 values is taken from a strongly right-skewed population. A histogram of the 200 sample values is most likely to be:
options: symmetric, because the sample is large
approximately normal, by the central limit theorem
questions.explanation: A large random sample tends to resemble the population it came from, so its values are right-skewed. The central limit theorem is about the distribution of sample means, not the values within one sample.

questions.stem: A farm's pumpkins have weights normally distributed with mean 13.5 kg and standard deviation 3 kg. For random samples of 15 pumpkins, the sample mean has:
questions.explanation: E(X̄) = μ = 13.5 and Var(X̄) = σ²/n = 9/15 = 0.6. Dividing σ rather than σ² by n gives 0.2, and 9 is the variance of a single pumpkin.

questions.stem: A population has standard deviation 10. For samples of size 25, the standard deviation of the sample mean is:
questions.explanation: Var(X̄) = σ²/n = 100/25 = 4, so the standard deviation is √4 = 2, which equals σ/√n. The value 4 is the variance, and 0.4 divides σ by n instead of √n.

questions.stem: If the sample size is multiplied by 4, the standard deviation of the sample mean is:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation of X̄ is σ/√n, and √(4n) = 2√n, so it is halved. The variance σ²/n is the quantity that is quartered.

questions.stem: A population has standard deviation 12. What sample size makes the standard deviation of the sample mean equal to 1.5?
questions.explanation: σ/√n = 1.5 gives √n = 12/1.5 = 8, so n = 64. Stopping at √n = 8 gives 8, which forgets to square.

questions.stem: The central limit theorem states that, for large enough n, the sample mean X̄ from a population with mean μ and variance σ² is:
options: exactly N(μ/n, σ²/n), whatever the population's distribution
approximately N(μ, σ²/n), whatever the population's distribution
approximately N(μ, σ²), whatever the population's distribution
approximately N(μ, σ²/n), but only if the population is normal
questions.explanation: The sample mean is centred on μ with variance σ²/n, and its distribution approaches a normal shape as n grows, even when the population is not normal. That last point is what makes the theorem so useful.

questions.stem: Waiting times at a clinic have a strongly right-skewed distribution. For random samples of 50 waiting times, the distribution of the sample mean is:
questions.explanation: By the central limit theorem, with n = 50 the sample mean is approximately normal regardless of the population's shape. The skewness of the population shows up in individual values, not in the sampling distribution of the mean.

questions.stem: A population has mean 200 and standard deviation 30. For random samples of 36, about 95% of sample means lie between:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation of X̄ is 30/√36 = 5, and about 95% of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean: 200 ± 10. Using σ = 30 itself gives 140 to 260.

questions.stem: Year 12 students' nightly sleep has mean 7.4 hours and standard deviation 2.4 hours. A random sample of 144 students is taken. Given P(Z < 2) ≈ 0.9772, the probability that the sample mean is under 7 hours is about:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation of X̄ is 2.4/√144 = 0.2, so z = (7 − 7.4)/0.2 = −2. P(Z < −2) = 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228. The value 0.0456 is the probability of being more than 2 standard deviations away on either side.

questions.stem: A population has mean 50 and standard deviation 8. A random sample of 64 is taken. Given P(Z < 1) ≈ 0.8413, the probability that the sample mean lies between 49 and 51 is about:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation of X̄ is 8/√64 = 1, so 49 and 51 correspond to z = −1 and z = 1. P(−1 < Z < 1) = 0.8413 − 0.1587 = 0.6826. The value 0.3413 covers only one side of the mean.

questions.stem: Each trial is a Bernoulli trial with p = 0.3. For samples of 84 trials, the sample mean (the proportion of successes) is approximately normal with mean 0.3 and standard deviation:
questions.explanation: The population is Bernoulli, with μ = 0.3 and σ² = 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.21. Then Var(X̄) = 0.21/84 = 0.0025, and the standard deviation is √0.0025 = 0.05. The value 0.0025 is the variance.
